After a couple weeks away and then a return to the task of caching blocks, I can report that the approach is working as expected.

text: After a couple weeks away and then a return to the task of caching blocks, I can report that the approach is working as expected.

elements.text:
It took some time to build up the infrastructure to reliably deserialize all aspects of a block into a custom allocator, however the amount of new code is very small, and the related changes to chain object deserialization are simple. Having done that it is now possible to destruct blocks on any thread without any memory deallocation cost whatsoever. The memory allocation cost is also close to zero.

In comparison to a full chain sync using the default memory allocator, the new custom linear allocator is slightly faster even when blocks are deallocated on the allocating thread. However when blocks are projected to a common strand for caching, the increased cost is only about 10%, none of which is in deallocation - just posting the closures to a work queue.

Previously, using the default memory allocator, the increased cost was totally prohibitive. The total run time went from about 60 minutes to at least 24 hours if not longer (never finished). So that aspect of the issue has been resolved.

The cost of using the custom allocator is a fixed memory allocation for each network thread, equal to the largest expected block object size possible. Some measurements demonstrated that all but 1 of the 840k blocks have an object size under 12MB (wire serialization is limited to 4MB).

Since each witness element is a smart pointer to byte vector, this more than doubles the typical object ratio. Not a problem for us, just need to get the max sizing correct.

elements.text:
There is a simple option here to conditionally (based on config) use the custom block allocator. This provides a modest performance advantage but may increase memory contention on smaller machines, haven't tested that yet.

But the objective was to take blocks that are downloaded, deserialized, checked, and stored concurrently across channels, and forward them to a common stranded handler for caching. This step cannot reasonably rely on the per-channel single block linear buffer, and expanding that buffer into a circular buffer presents the same ultimate limits and more complexity.

However, once a block is deserialized using the custom allocator, all of its many thousands of individual allocations comprise a single contiguous memory block. This means that the block object also can be copied and serialized (e.g. to/from disk) at almost no cost.

elements.text: So, in order to achieve the objective with minimal cost and complexity, I'm planning to allocate a chunk of memory equal to the deserialized block and copy the block into it. Freeing this allocation consists only of calling
free(ptr)
on this one
shared_ptr<block>

, which will be constructed with a deleter that simply calls free on its own address and otherwise does nothing (e.g. no destructors get invoked). This is possible because all objects contained within a block have only default destructors with the exception of
std::shared_ptr
and
std::vector

and these only invoke other destructors and/or free the same underlying memory.

Since the objects are all const there is no downstream risk apart from metadata setters, though these should only be used by the code that allocates the block in the first place.

Note that block destruct is 7% of the run cost, even without memory deallocations. So this will more than offset the alloc/copy cost of the implementation.

elements.text: So after every block is copied to its new buffer, which requires only a single
malloc(size)
and
copy_n(size)

, the fixed per-channel block linear allocator just resets back to its buffer start, as it does now. This allows me to remove the tracking shared_ptr that was retained in each block, for the purpose of holding a mutex to block use of the buffer until the block is deleted. Now the block simply lives as long as it wants and deletes its memory when the shared pointer refcount goes to zero. So much simpler.

elements.text:
Basically we get super-efficient and simple block object allocation and free deallocation. No custom memory allocator can beat a single-threaded linear allocator, as it's just a couple of math ops. We can then move the blocks across threads at zero additional deallocation cost, where previously that cost was entirely prohibitive, and don't even have to worry about deallocation order.

One side benefit, we now also have a precise and free measurement of the allocated size of block objects (the only ones that really matter). We can also apply this same allocation strategy to block and prevout deserialization from the store for the purpose of validation (in the case where the block object or prevout isn't cached).

elements.text: The problem I reported on July 2 is now finally resolved. The objective is to be able to cache downloaded blocks for validation so that they don't have to be read back out of the store to create the partial ordering when validating. This goes back to the v4 redesign work in 2021. The problem was memory deallocation, which was explosive and entirely prohibitive. Allocating and deallocating thousands of small chunks on the same threads is not a problem, but deallocating them on a different thread creates heavy contention, increasing sync time by an order of magnitude. This collection of blocks into a strand for caching is necessary in order to implement it in a lock-free manner. This therefore implies block destruction in distinct threads from block allocation...

elements.text: Internally, thread safe allocators (like new/delete) have to sequence access to the single memory resource. They optimize this by taking smaller chunks from a per-thread larger allocation. So that's very efficient. But when it comes time to free the memory, and you aren't on the thread that allocated it, that can be expensive (like a lock). With little contention it's fine, but this is deallocating millions of little chunks per second.

text: After some refactoring and a new release build run with the debugger attached, I hit a break  in `witness` deserialization. There was a change to deserialization such that a byte vector (`data_chunk`) is allocated by the stream reader and returned as a raw pointer. This was immediately assigned to a `shared_ptr`, which will accept either a `nullptr` (`shared_ptr.empty()`) or a pointer to the `data_chunk` object. The pointer is then dereferenced, which is a segfault if the value was `nullptr`. So just needed to check the return value of the pointer or `(bool)reader` and exist the witness reader early.

elements.text: The change was done to allow the vector to be created by the allocator instead of being returned as stack-allocated. The failure would only reproduce when an invalid block was received, and happened to attempt witness deserialization while the stream was invalid. This is pretty common, and there is no early termination of deserialization due to invalidity, as this would introduce a lot of additional conditions.
